overview.what_it_is: This review joins measurement, fractions, ratio, shapes, and arithmetic.

format_facts.label: Main skills
format_facts.value: Rounding, unit changes, fractions, ratio, area, and volume

format_facts.label: Units used
format_facts.value: Miles, yards, feet, inches, pounds, ounces, gallons, quarts, and cups

format_facts.label: Question types
format_facts.value: Short sums, unit questions, shape problems, and word problems

format_facts.label: Best tools
format_facts.value: Unit facts, bar models, diagrams, and careful checking

scoring_factors.name: Correct method
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the right steps were chosen.

scoring_factors.name: Correct units
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the answer uses the needed unit.

scoring_factors.name: Accurate arithmetic
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether each number step is correct.

scoring_factors.name: Complete working
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether important steps are clearly shown.

scoring_factors.name: Reasonable answer
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the answer fits the question.

critical_rules: Change quantities into matching units before comparing them.
Write square units for area and cubic units for volume.
Carry extra small units into the larger unit.
Change mixed units into one small unit before dividing.
Use the same ratio order as the question.
Read the rounding place before checking the next digit.
State the final answer with its unit.

learning_goals: You will round whole numbers to the nearest hundred.
You will round decimals to one decimal place.
You will change yards, feet, and inches.
You will change pounds and ounces.
You will change gallons, quarts, and cups.
You will find a fraction of a quantity.
You will find a whole from a known fraction.
You will solve ratio problems with rectangles.
You will find perimeter, area, and volume.
You will multiply and divide compound units.

core_method.name: Read → Recall → Match units → Model → Work → Rename → Check
core_method.summary: First read the unit. Then make units match. Work carefully.

steps.detail: Underline the numbers, units, and question words.
Write the unit fact needed for the problem.
Change all amounts into useful matching units.
Draw bars or a shape when relationships matter.
Complete one clear arithmetic step at a time.
Change the result into the requested compound unit.
Check size, unit, and each operation.

techniques.name: Build a unit ladder
techniques.purpose: It helps you move between linked units.
how_to: Write the unit fact before starting.
Multiply when changing into smaller units.
Divide when changing into larger units.
Rename any leftover part carefully.
techniques.why_it_matters: It stops you from using the wrong operation.
techniques.common_error: Dividing when changing to a smaller unit.

techniques.name: Use one small unit
techniques.purpose: It makes compound-unit arithmetic much easier.
how_to: Choose the smaller unit shown.
Change every part into that unit.
Do the multiplication or division.
Change the answer back when asked.
techniques.example: $2\text{ ft }8\text{ in}=24\text{ in}+8\text{ in}=32\text{ in}$, then $32\text{ in}\div4=8\text{ in}$.
techniques.why_it_matters: One unit avoids carrying errors during division.

techniques.name: Find a fraction of an amount
techniques.purpose: It finds a chosen part of a quantity.
how_to: Divide by the bottom number first.
Multiply by the top number next.
Keep the unit with the answer.
Check whether the answer is sensible.
techniques.why_it_matters: Dividing first often keeps numbers small.

techniques.name: Find the whole amount
techniques.purpose: It finds a total from one known fraction.
how_to: Draw equal bars for the bottom number.
Mark how many bars are known.
Find the amount in one bar.
Multiply by the total number of bars.
techniques.example: If $\frac{2}{3}$ is $6\text{ c}$, then $6\div2=3\text{ c}$ and $3\times3=9\text{ c}$.
techniques.why_it_matters: The bar model shows why each step works.
techniques.common_error: Finding another fraction instead of the whole.

techniques.name: Use ratio units
techniques.purpose: It finds missing lengths from a ratio.
how_to: Draw bars in the given ratio.
Match the known amount to its bars.
Find the value of one ratio unit.
Find each missing amount.
techniques.example: For length to width $5:2$, $30\text{ yd}\div5=6\text{ yd}$ per unit.
techniques.why_it_matters: It keeps the ratio order clear.
techniques.common_error: Switching the length and width parts.

techniques.name: Separate shape formulas
techniques.purpose: It prevents mixing perimeter, area, and volume.
how_to: Decide what the question asks.
Use lengths for perimeter.
Use square units for area.
Use cubic units for volume.
techniques.example: A cube with side $6\text{ in}$ has volume $6\times6\times6=216\text{ in}^3$.
techniques.why_it_matters: Each measure describes a different feature.
techniques.common_error: Writing square units for a volume answer.

techniques.name: Round using the next digit
techniques.purpose: It gives the requested nearby value.
how_to: Find the digit in the rounding place.
Look at the digit just after it.
Keep the digit if the next is below five.
Raise it by one if the next is five or more.
techniques.example: $258.76\text{ lb}\approx258.8\text{ lb}$ to one decimal place.
techniques.why_it_matters: Only the next digit decides the rounding.

techniques.name: Compare using one unit
techniques.purpose: It makes unlike measurements easy to order.
how_to: Choose one shared unit.
Change every amount into that unit.
Compare the new numbers.
Give the answer in its original form.
techniques.example: $2.5\text{ ft}=30\text{ in}$ and $0.5\text{ yd}=18\text{ in}$, so $37\text{ in}$ is greatest.
techniques.why_it_matters: The numbers cannot be compared fairly before conversion.

worked_examples.title: Share cloth using feet and inches
worked_examples.input: Share $5\text{ yd}$ of cloth equally among $12$ napkins.
worked_examples.decoding: The answer must be in feet and inches.
worked_examples.plan: Change yards to feet. Divide. Rename the fraction of a foot.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar model has $12$ equal parts. The whole bar is $5\text{ yd}$. First change yards into feet: $5\text{ yd}=5\times3\text{ ft}=15\text{ ft}$. Share the cloth: $15\text{ ft}\div12=1\frac{3}{12}\text{ ft}=1\frac{1}{4}\text{ ft}$. Now change $\frac{1}{4}\text{ ft}$ into inches: $12\text{ in}\div4=3\text{ in}$. Each napkin used $1\text{ ft }3\text{ in}$ of cloth.

annotations.comment: Feet are easier to share than yards.
The result includes one whole foot.
One foot has twelve inches.
The answer uses the requested compound unit.

worked_examples.title: Find one share in ounces
worked_examples.input: An $8\text{ lb}$ crate is divided into $12$ equal shares.
worked_examples.decoding: Pounds must change into ounces before dividing.
worked_examples.plan: Change the whole weight into ounces. Then share equally.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar model has $12$ equal parts. The whole bar weighs $8\text{ lb}$. Change pounds into ounces: $8\text{ lb}=8\times16\text{ oz}=128\text{ oz}$. Divide by the number of shares: $128\text{ oz}\div12=10\text{ r }8\text{ oz}$. The remainder is $8\text{ oz}$ out of another group of $12\text{ oz}$, so it is $\frac{8}{12}\text{ oz}=\frac{2}{3}\text{ oz}$. Each share weighs $10\frac{2}{3}\text{ oz}$.

annotations.comment: Changing to ounces gives one useful unit.
The remainder must not be lost.
The leftover part is written in simplest form.
The answer is a mixed number.

worked_examples.title: Find a rectangle from its ratio
worked_examples.input: A field has length to width ratio $5:2$. Its length is $30\text{ yd}$.
worked_examples.decoding: Five ratio parts represent the known length.
worked_examples.plan: Find one ratio unit. Then find width, perimeter, and area.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar model has $5$ length parts and $2$ width parts. The $5$ length parts total $30\text{ yd}$. One ratio unit is $30\text{ yd}\div5=6\text{ yd}$. The width is $2\times6\text{ yd}=12\text{ yd}$. The perimeter is $2\times(30\text{ yd}+12\text{ yd})=2\times42\text{ yd}=84\text{ yd}$. The area is $30\text{ yd}\times12\text{ yd}=360\text{ yd}^2$. The field has perimeter $84\text{ yd}$ and area $360\text{ yd}^2$.

annotations.comment: This finds one equal ratio part.
The width uses two ratio parts.
Perimeter measures all four sides.
Area measures the space inside.

worked_examples.title: Multiply gallons and quarts
worked_examples.decoding: Multiply both parts. Then carry groups of four quarts.
worked_examples.plan: Multiply gallons and quarts. Rename extra quarts as gallons.
worked_examples.model_answer: Multiply the gallons: $4\text{ gal}\times5=20\text{ gal}$. Multiply the quarts: $3\text{ qt}\times5=15\text{ qt}$. Rename the quarts: $15\text{ qt}=3\text{ gal }3\text{ qt}$ because $4\text{ qt}=1\text{ gal}$. Add the gallon parts: $20\text{ gal}+3\text{ gal }3\text{ qt}=23\text{ gal }3\text{ qt}$. The answer is $23\text{ gal }3\text{ qt}$.

annotations.comment: The small-unit part is multiplied too.
Every four quarts makes one gallon.
The carried gallons join the first product.
The small part is less than one gallon.

worked_examples.title: Find a whole jug from two thirds
worked_examples.input: $\frac{2}{3}$ of a jug contains $6\text{ c}$. Find the whole amount.
worked_examples.decoding: Two equal parts hold six cups. Three parts make the whole.
worked_examples.plan: Find one bar part. Then find all three parts.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar model has $3$ equal parts. Two parts total $6\text{ c}$. One part is $6\text{ c}\div2=3\text{ c}$. The whole has three parts: $3\text{ c}\times3=9\text{ c}$. The jug holds $9\text{ c}$ of water.

annotations.comment: This finds the amount in one part.
The whole contains three equal parts.
The answer is larger than the known fraction.
The bars show why division comes first.

worked_examples.title: Correct a gallon and cup mistake
worked_examples.input: Express $2\frac{1}{4}\text{ gal}$ in gallons and cups.
worked_examples.decoding: Only the fractional gallon must change into cups.
worked_examples.plan: Keep two gallons. Change one quarter gallon into cups.
worked_examples.model_answer: Keep the whole part as $2\text{ gal}$. One gallon equals $4\text{ qt}$, and one quart equals $4\text{ c}$. Therefore, $1\text{ gal}=4\times4\text{ c}=16\text{ c}$. Find one quarter of a gallon: $\frac{1}{4}\times16\text{ c}=4\text{ c}$. So $2\frac{1}{4}\text{ gal}=2\text{ gal }4\text{ c}$. The correct answer is $2\text{ gal }4\text{ c}$.

annotations.comment: This joins the two capacity facts.
One quarter gallon is four cups.
The whole gallons stay unchanged.
One cup would be only one sixteenth gallon.

worked_examples.title: Find Ashley's weight
worked_examples.input: Three children weigh $243\text{ lb}$. Morgan is $30\text{ lb}$ heavier than Emily. Ashley is $6\text{ lb}$ heavier than Emily.
worked_examples.decoding: Each weight can be built from Emily's weight.
worked_examples.plan: Remove the extra parts. Divide the equal parts by three.
worked_examples.model_answer: The bar model gives Emily one equal bar. Ashley has the same bar plus $6\text{ lb}$. Morgan has the same bar plus $30\text{ lb}$. Remove the extra weights: $243\text{ lb}-30\text{ lb}-6\text{ lb}=207\text{ lb}$. These are three equal base bars. Emily weighs $207\text{ lb}\div3=69\text{ lb}$. Ashley weighs $69\text{ lb}+6\text{ lb}=75\text{ lb}$. Ashley weighs $75\text{ lb}$.

annotations.comment: This is Morgan's extra part.
This is Ashley's extra part.
The remaining weight forms three equal bars.
Ashley has Emily's weight plus six pounds.

items.when_to_use: Use it for an answer found by multiplying.
Use it for an answer found by dividing.
Use it for an amount left after division.
Use it when amounts must be added.
It shows how many equal parts are chosen.
It is the bottom number showing all equal parts.
Use it for a whole amount and a fraction.
Use it when the fraction cannot be reduced more.
It means change a measure into another unit.
Use it for measures like feet and inches.
Use it for how much liquid a container holds.
Use it for pounds and ounces.
Use it for the distance around a shape.
Use it for the space inside a flat shape.
Use it for space inside a solid shape.
Use it when writing a volume answer.
It tells you to divide into equal shares.
With fractions, it usually means multiply.
It shows one amount is smaller by a difference.
Use it to compare amounts in a fixed order.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing feet, inches, and yards without changing units.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The printed numbers do not show equal-sized units.
common_mistakes.fix: Change every length into one shared unit first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing both parts of a compound measure separately.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Small units may need regrouping before division.
common_mistakes.fix: Change the whole amount into the smaller unit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to carry extra ounces, inches, or quarts.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The small-unit part becomes too large.
common_mistakes.fix: Trade each full group for one larger unit.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Square units measure area, not solid space.
common_mistakes.fix: Use cubic units after multiplying three lengths.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Perimeter is only a length around a shape.
common_mistakes.fix: Write a plain length unit for perimeter.

common_mistakes.mistake: Switching the order of a ratio.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The bars then represent the wrong quantities.
common_mistakes.fix: Write labels above the ratio parts.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The answer may round to the wrong place.
common_mistakes.fix: Circle the rounding place and check the next digit.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Part of the measured amount disappears.
common_mistakes.fix: Write the remainder as a fraction of one share.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A gallon contains $16\text{ c}$, not $4\text{ c}$.

time_budget.focus: Recall length, weight, and capacity facts.
Use bars to find parts and wholes.
Multiply, divide, carry, and rename units.
Solve word problems and check all answers.

drills.name: Unit fact cards
drills.instructions: Write one unit fact on each card. Test both directions.

drills.name: One-unit race
drills.instructions: Change ten compound measures into their smaller units.

drills.name: Fraction bars
drills.instructions: Draw bars for four fraction-of-quantity questions.

drills.name: Find the whole
drills.instructions: Solve four problems where one fraction is known.

drills.name: Shape check
drills.instructions: Label each answer as length, square units, or cubic units.

drills.name: Carry and rename
drills.instructions: Multiply six compound measures. Rename every oversized part.

drills.name: Compare fairly
drills.instructions: Change five mixed-unit choices into one shared unit.

drills.name: Error detective
drills.instructions: Find and fix four wrong measurement solutions.

practice_plan.routine: Recall the unit fact. Draw when needed. Work carefully. Check units.

mastery_checklist: I can round a whole number to the nearest hundred.
I can round a decimal to one decimal place.
I can change yards, feet, and inches.
I can change pounds and ounces.
I can change gallons, quarts, and cups.
I can compare measures by using one unit.
I can find a fraction of a quantity.
I can find a whole from a known fraction.
I can use ratio bars to find a missing length.
I can find perimeter and use length units.
I can find area and use square units.
I can find volume and use cubic units.
I can multiply compound measures and carry units.
I can divide compound measures using one small unit.
I can state each final answer with its unit.
strategy_notes: Write the needed unit fact beside each question.
Estimate the answer before completing long working.
Use inches, ounces, or cups when division is difficult.
Draw ratio bars before using the given length.
Circle whether the question asks perimeter, area, or volume.
Check that a small-unit remainder stays below one large unit.
For comparisons, ignore the choices until units match.
Read the requested answer unit before starting.
Use inverse operations to check multiplication and division.
Check that a fraction of an amount has a sensible size.
